summary: A week after His resurrection Jesus appears again with Thomas present, offers him the proof he demanded, and Thomas confesses, “My Lord and my God!”
key_insight: Jesus answered Thomas in Thomas’s own words: finger, hands, hand, side. He knew exactly what Thomas had said when He was not visibly present. And John never says Thomas touched Him; meeting Jesus was enough.
story: Eight days later the disciples were again inside, and this time Thomas was with them. The doors were shut, yet Jesus came and stood in the midst and said, “Peace to you!”
Then He said to Thomas, “Reach your finger here, and look at My hands; and reach your hand here, and put it into My side. Do not be unbelieving, but believing.”
Thomas answered Him, “My Lord and my God!”
Jesus said to him, “Thomas, because you have seen Me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”

Jesus did many other signs in the presence of His disciples, which are not written in this book; “but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in His name.”

scene.label: After eight days
scene.text: People counted both the first and last day, so this was most likely the next Sunday, one week after the resurrection. Again the disciples met on the first day of the week, the day the church came to call the Lord’s Day (probably what John means in Revelation 1:10).

scene.label: Thomas before Easter
scene.text: John shows Thomas as loyal and blunt. When Jesus set out for Judea, Thomas said, “Let us also go, that we may die with Him” (John 11:16). In the upper room he asked plainly, “how can we know the way?” (John 14:5).

scene.label: The wound in His side
scene.text: Only John records that a soldier “pierced His side with a spear” (John 19:34). That is why Thomas speaks of putting his hand into Jesus’ side, and why Jesus invites him to do it.

scene.label: “My Lord and my God”
scene.text: The words echo the psalmist’s prayer to the LORD, “my God and my Lord” (Psalm 35:23). Thomas, a Jew who confessed that God is one, speaks these words to Jesus, and Jesus accepts them.

scene.label: Many other signs
scene.text: John says plainly that he chose. He tells only a handful of Jesus’ miracles, often counted as seven before the cross, from the water made wine at Cana to the raising of Lazarus, and he calls them signs: deeds that point to who Jesus is. The first, he says, “manifested His glory” (John 2:11).

witnesses.john: John alone tells of Thomas. He began his Gospel by saying that “the Word was God” (1:1), and here the last of the eleven to believe says to Jesus, “My Lord and my God!” Then John names what his whole Gospel has set out to show: that Jesus is “the Christ, the Son of God.”

seeing.reveals: Jesus is Lord and God, and He does not despise an honest doubter. He comes back for one man, meets him at the point of his doubt, and receives the highest confession in the Gospels.
seeing.living: Thomas stayed with the disciples through a week of doubt, and that is where Jesus met him. No one today can see the nail prints, but Jesus has already blessed those who believe without seeing, through the testimony of those who did. Bring your questions to Him honestly, and let them end where Thomas’s ended: in worship.
seeing.ponder: Is Jesus only “Lord” to you in a general sense, or can you say to Him with Thomas, “My Lord and my God”?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus meets honest doubt with Himself, and doubt becomes worship.
outline: A Savior who comes back for one (26–27)
A confession that says it all (28)
A blessing for those who have not seen (29–31)
preaching.watch_for: Jesus’ blessing in verse 29 is for people who were not in the room, and John turns to them at once: these signs “are written that you may believe” (20:31). The reader who believes without seeing is the one Jesus calls blessed.

title: Jesus and Thomas
